title: Tilda and the Lost Banner
markdown:
In the sun-drenched realm of Greenleaf lived Tilda, a tabby of marmalade and cream, whose emerald eyes missed little. Shadows and tight dark places were not her kingdom. Window sills were. Forgotten shoeboxes made her flinch.

One dewy morning a hush fell. The Beetle King wailed. His Royal Banner of the Crimson Clover was lost: spider silk, embroidered with dawn’s first light, the heart of beetlekind. Without it the Great Gathering would be a dismal affair of empty poles and drooping antennae.

The King summoned Birch, the knightly beetle, gleaming in mist-polished armor. “I shall find the banner.”

Birch knew the trail led to the Whispering Rosebush, a maze of thorns and shade. Who could navigate such a place? Someone swift and stealthy, with eyes that pierced gloom.

“Tilda. Your kingdom calls.”

Tilda, mid-nap, blinked. A quest? She, who treated the space under the dresser as an optional country?

Birch explained the plight, the banner’s weight, the journey. “But the tunnels,” Tilda murmured, tail twitching, “are so small. And so very dark.”

Birch’s gaze was kind. He did not give a lecture. He mentioned the King, the Gathering, and, almost as an afterthought, an extra sardine ration. The sardine was not nothing. Birch’s faith was more.

“Very well, Sir Knight.” She stood, tail high. “I shall guide you.”

The rosebush yawned, a maw of thorns. Tilda’s fur bristled with something that was not only fear. Birch clung to her back. “Swiftly and surely.”

She thought of the King, of trust, of the delectable extra. She pictured the banner coming home. Then she leaped into the thorny embrace.

Inside: a tapestry of green and brown, vines as arches, rose-scent humming. Tilda moved like a shadow through narrow paths. Birch sniffed the trail, keen as a compass with legs.

A low slimy sound. “Who goes there?” Bartholomew the Snail blocked the way, eyestalks considering them as if they were Tuesday’s weather.

“We seek the Beetle King’s banner,” Birch announced.

Bartholomew sighed and pointed. “Saw something bright flutter by, caught by Ol’ Silas, the spider. Up that way. Mind the web. Stickier than my Tuesday breakfast.”

Tilda swallowed. Spiders. The banner was near. She thanked Bartholomew, who resumed his ponderous crawl. Fear stayed a tiny knot. Determination grew a little fire.

They reached a vast opening lit by glowing moss. There, draped in a colossal web, fluttered the Crimson Clover Banner. Above it, eight beady eyes. Silas the Spider surveyed his domain as if the silk were a ledger.

“Now,” Birch whispered, “quick and clever.”

Tilda eyed banner, web, spider. Purpose argued with the old flinch. A plan bloomed that did not need a speech: outwit, do not wrestle.

She zipped around the web’s edge, a blur of orange and cream. Instincts sang. Sharp claws snagged a loose thread near the banner’s tie. Nimble leaps, careful twists: she loosened the anchors, a dancer unpicking a knot.

Silas was baffled. He had never met such a swift attacker. A final tug. The banner came free and landed softly at Birch’s feet.

“Victory,” Birch cried, hoisting it, which from a beetle is still quite a hoist.

The journey back was bright. Tilda navigated the tunnels with a confidence that surprised her own whiskers. The rosebush was still a rosebush. It was also a path she now knew.

They emerged into sun. Cheers. The Beetle King beamed. “Tilda of the Sunbeam.”

Warmth spread, hotter than any sill. Fear had not vanished. It had been outrun for an afternoon. That night she savored a magnificent sardine and did not explain it to anyone. The banner hung where beetlekind could see it, and the shoebox under the dresser remained optional.
